Stage 3 · Reading

The kitchen with the yellow door

One vivid childhood memory, one box of photographs, and what the research says about being certain.

🚪📸
1 · Before you read. How reliable do you think your own earliest memory is?

Choose one and say why. Compare with a partner before you read.Choose one and say why before you read.Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

The kitchen with the yellow door

Written for this course. Research finding from Talarico & Rubin, ‘Confidence, not consistency, characterizes flashbulb memories’, Psychological Science 14(5), 2003.

1I can recall it very clearly. I am four, sitting under the table in my grandmother’s kitchen, and the door to the yard is yellow. She is cutting something on the board above me and the radio keeps stopping. I remember hearing her laugh at whatever the radio said, and I remember deciding not to come out.

2For thirty years I enjoyed telling that story. It is a vivid memory, one of maybe six that survive from my childhood, and vivid memories feel reliable, so I never bothered to check it. It was one of the few things I could offer when people asked about my childhood, and I told it the same way every time, which I now understand is exactly the problem: each telling was a copy of the last one rather than a return to the kitchen. Then last spring my aunt began sorting through the photographs, and I stopped believing my own account within about a minute.

3The door was green. It had always been green, and it was painted yellow in 1998, when I was twenty-two. My aunt has no recollection of any radio in that kitchen; my mother vaguely remembers one, but in the other house. I just about remember the yard and have no memory whatsoever of the room beside it; shown the photographs, I managed to identify the table at once and nothing else. What everybody agrees on is that table, and the fact that I refused to come out from under it.

4None of this makes me unusual, and the tidiest evidence for that comes from a study that had nothing to do with kitchens. On 12 September 2001, fifty-four students at an American university were asked to write down what they remembered of hearing the previous day’s news, and also what they remembered of an ordinary event from the same week. They were tested again up to thirty-two weeks later. Both sets of memories lost consistent details at the same rate and picked up inconsistent ones at the same rate. Dramatic memories were not more accurate.

5What did differ was confidence. Ratings of vividness, of recollection and of belief in one’s own accuracy declined for the everyday memories and stayed high for the dramatic ones. The students went on being certain about the memory that was decaying exactly as fast as the one they had stopped trusting, and most of them would have refused to accept that their own account had changed at all. The researchers put it plainly: such memories are not special in their accuracy, only in their perceived accuracy. That is a slightly frightening sentence, because it removes the one test most of us use.

6I have stopped claiming the yellow door and I still see it. That is the part that unsettles me: knowing a detail is invented does not make it disappear. Psychologists will tell you that a memory has begun to fade the first time it is recalled, that memories are rebuilt rather than replayed, that the brain prefers to invent a plausible detail rather than to leave a gap, and that a photograph reminds you of the last telling rather than of the day. I believe them. I would just like to remember that kitchen once without the door.

Text A · The door was green

Written for this course.

I can recall it very clearly. I am four, sitting under the table in my grandmother’s kitchen, and the door to the yard is yellow. She is cutting something on the board above me and the radio keeps stopping. I remember hearing her laugh at whatever the radio said, and I remember deciding not to come out.

For thirty years I enjoyed telling that story. It is a vivid memory, one of maybe six that survive from my childhood, and vivid memories feel reliable, so I never bothered to check it. It was one of the few things I could offer when people asked about my childhood, and I told it the same way every time, which I now understand is exactly the problem: each telling was a copy of the last one rather than a return to the kitchen. Then last spring my aunt began sorting through the photographs, and I stopped believing my own account within about a minute.

The door was green. It had always been green, and it was painted yellow in 1998, when I was twenty-two. My aunt has no recollection of any radio in that kitchen; my mother vaguely remembers one, but in the other house. I just about remember the yard and have no memory whatsoever of the room beside it; shown the photographs, I managed to identify the table at once and nothing else. What everybody agrees on is that table, and the fact that I refused to come out from under it. Nobody in the family has tried to persuade me that the rest of it happened, which I notice I would have preferred.

Text B · Certain, and wrong

Written for this course, from Talarico & Rubin, Psychological Science 14(5), 2003.

None of this makes me unusual, and the tidiest evidence for that comes from a study that had nothing to do with kitchens. I have stopped claiming the yellow door and I still see it. That is the part that unsettles me: knowing a detail is invented does not make it disappear. 1 · Read the explanation.
What follows a verb, and why

Three groups, and one short list to learn. Some verbs are always followed by -ing: enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, imagine, deny, suggest, keep, practise, miss. Some are always followed by to + verb: want, hope, decide, refuse, promise, offer, manage, afford, bother, seem. There is no logic worth hunting for; the pattern is stored with the verb.

With an object. A group of verbs takes a person and then to: ask, tell, remind, advise, allow, expect, want. She reminded me to bring it, never she reminded me bringing it.

Either form, no real difference. Begin, start, continue, like, love, hate, prefer: She began sorting and She began to sort are both correct. After a continuous tense, the infinitive is preferred: It is starting to rain.

Either form, different meaning. This is the part that matters. Remember doing is a memory; remember to do is a task. Stop doing ends an activity; stop to do means you paused for a purpose. Try doing is an experiment; try to do is an attempt at something difficult. Forget doing is about the past, forget to do about a duty missed. Regret doing looks back; regret to say introduces bad news.

Negatives and passives. The negative goes in front: I remember not coming out, I decided not to say anything. Both forms have passives: I hate being interrupted, I expected to be told.

The commonest errors at this level
  • I enjoy to read, I avoid to go, I finished to write.
  • I decided going, I want going, I managed opening it.
  • She reminded me bringing it.
  • I stopped to smoke when you mean you gave up.
  • I remember to lock the door when you mean you remember doing it.

Two things to watch

1 — The meaning pairs are worth memorising. Remember, stop, try, forget, regret: five verbs, and each one says something different depending on what follows it.

2 — Suggest is the trap. I suggest going or I suggest that we go, never I suggest to go.

5 · Worked example. Read it before you do the exercises.
Choosing between the two forms

The sentence: I remember ______ the door. Both locking and to lock are grammatical, so the choice is about meaning.

Step 1 — ask which came first. If the locking happened and you are recalling it, the memory comes second: I remember locking the door.

Step 2 — check the alternative. Remember to lock the door puts the remembering first and the locking afterwards: a task, usually as an instruction.

Step 3 — test it in context. I remember ______ the door, so it cannot have been me who left it open. That is an argument about the past, so: locking.

Step 4 — do the same with the other pairs. Stop, try and forget work the same way: ask whether the second verb has already happened or is still to come.

13 · Read this before the extra practice.
Three groups, and only one of them has to be learned

Always -ing: enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, imagine, deny, suggest, keep, practise, miss — I enjoyed telling it. Suggest is the one people get wrong most often: she suggested to check → she suggested checking.

Always to: want, hope, decide, refuse, promise, offer, manage, afford, bother, seem — I never bothered to check. Several of these carry meaning worth noticing: manage to means you succeeded with difficulty, and bother to means you made the effort at all.

Object + to: ask, tell, want, remind, advise, allow, expect — She reminded me to bring it. The person comes first, then to.

Either, with no difference: begin, start, continue, like, love, hate, prefer — She began sorting and She began to sort say the same thing.

The four verbs where the form is the meaning

remember: I remember locking the door — the memory of a past act; Remember to lock the door — a task ahead of you. forget mirrors it: I will never forget seeing it (memory) against I forgot to lock it (task not done).

stop: He stopped smoking — he gave it up; He stopped to smoke — he paused in order to have one. The second is a purpose infinitive, which is why the meanings are so far apart.

try: Try turning it off — an experiment, easy to do, and it might solve the problem; I tried to open it — an attempt at something difficult, and it may have failed.

A quick test for the memory verbs: if the event came before the remembering, use -ing; if it comes after, use to.

Errors to watch: She suggested to check → checking · I avoid to talk about it → talking · I managed opening it → to open · She reminded to me to bring it → reminded me to.

1 · Read the model.
Model · a memory in four paragraphs

I am five, and I am standing in the corridor of a train. It is dark outside and the window is cold against my forehead. My father is holding a paper cup of tea that he keeps moving from hand to hand because it is too hot, and somebody down the carriage is laughing at something I cannot hear. I remember deciding that I would stay there until the light came back.

I can recall it very clearly, and I have told it perhaps fifty times. It is one of maybe four memories that survive from my childhood, and like most vivid memories it feels completely reliable from the inside.

My father has no recollection of the tea. He does remember the train, and he says we took it three times, which means I cannot identify which journey I am seeing. My mother vaguely remembers a corridor, and she thinks I was seven rather than five. Nobody but me remembers the laughing, and I would not now swear to it: the brain will invent a plausible detail rather than leave a gap, and laughter in the dark is exactly the kind of thing it invents.

What survives all three accounts is the train, the dark and my refusal to sit down. The rest has begun to fade, or was never there. I have stopped defending the cup of tea, and I have not managed to stop seeing it.
